tool.name: GitLab CI/CD
tool.tagline: GitLab's built-in pipelines: build, test and deploy from .gitlab-ci.yml
tool.description: GitLab CI/CD runs pipelines defined in a .gitlab-ci.yml file at the root of a GitLab repository. Jobs are grouped into stages, executed by runners (usually inside Docker images), and can pass artifacts, deploy to environments and trigger other pipelines. It is the standard way to automate builds, tests and deployments for teams that host their code on GitLab.com or a self-managed GitLab.

concepts.name: Pipelines, stages, jobs and runners
concepts.summary: The building blocks of GitLab CI/CD: a pipeline of stages, each holding jobs, executed by runners.
concepts.why: Every .gitlab-ci.yml is written in these terms, and they decide what runs in parallel and where.
concepts.body:
A **pipeline** is one execution of your CI/CD configuration, created when you push, open a merge request, run a schedule or click **Run pipeline**. It is defined in `.gitlab-ci.yml` at the repository root.

A pipeline consists of **jobs**: named units of work, each with a `script` of shell commands. Jobs are grouped into **stages** that run in order: by default `build`, then `test`, then `deploy`, with hidden `.pre` and `.post` stages at the very start and end. All jobs in one stage run in parallel; the next stage starts only when every job of the previous stage has succeeded. A job without a `stage` goes into `test`.

Jobs are executed by **runners**: agents that poll GitLab for work. GitLab.com provides hosted runners; companies often register their own. Most runners use the Docker executor, so each job runs in a fresh container from the image you choose.

The pipeline graph, job logs, test reports and artifacts appear in the GitLab UI under **Build, Pipelines**. The pipeline status is attached to the commit and to merge requests, where it can be required to pass before merging.

Because each job starts in a clean container, jobs share nothing by default: files must be passed with artifacts or cache, which you will learn shortly.
concepts.code:
# .gitlab-ci.yml : three stages, four jobs
stages: [build, test, deploy]

build-app:
  stage: build
  script: echo "compiling"

unit-tests:            # these two run in parallel
  stage: test
  script: echo "unit tests"
lint:
  stage: test
  script: echo "linting"

deploy-prod:           # starts after both test jobs pass
  stage: deploy
  script: echo "deploying"
takeaways: A pipeline has stages; a stage has jobs; runners execute jobs
Jobs in a stage run in parallel; stages run in order
Each job starts in a clean environment
pitfalls: Assuming a file created in the build job is automatically present in the test job.

quiz.q: A job in the test stage fails. What happens to jobs in the deploy stage?
options: They run only if allow_failure is set on deploy
They run in parallel with test
quiz.explain: A stage starts only after all jobs of the previous stage succeeded (unless failures are allowed).

concepts.name: Your first .gitlab-ci.yml
concepts.summary: Write a pipeline that installs dependencies and runs tests in a Docker image, then watch it run after a push.
concepts.why: A green pipeline on every push is the first step to reliable merges.
concepts.body:
Create `.gitlab-ci.yml` in the repository root, commit and push. GitLab parses it and creates a pipeline immediately; syntax errors are reported on the pipeline page, and the **Pipeline editor** (Build, Pipeline editor) validates the file as you type.

A job is a top-level key that is not a reserved keyword. The essentials:

- `script`: one command or a list of commands run by the runner's shell. If any command exits non-zero, the job fails.
- `image`: the Docker image the job runs in, such as `python:3.13` or `node:22`.
- `before_script` and `after_script`: commands run before and after `script`. `after_script` runs even when the job fails, in a separate shell.
- `default:` sets keywords like `image` and `before_script` for every job.

Each job starts with the repository already cloned into `$CI_PROJECT_DIR`, so there is no checkout step to write; GitLab fetches the commit for you (shallow by default, 20 commits).

Keep YAML strings safe: a command containing `: ` (colon and space) or starting with special characters needs quotes, or the line is parsed as a mapping. When in doubt, quote the whole command.
concepts.code:
default:
  image: python:3.13-slim

stages: [test]

test:
  stage: test
  before_script:
    - pip install -r requirements.txt
  script:
    - python -m pytest -q        # 12 passed in 0.8s
    - "echo 'Result: done'"      # quoted because of the colon-space
  after_script:
    - echo "always runs, even on failure"
takeaways: Commit .gitlab-ci.yml at the root and push to start a pipeline
script is required; image picks the container
Code is already checked out into $CI_PROJECT_DIR
pitfalls: Unquoted commands containing ': ' break the YAML.

quiz.q: Your job's second script command fails. What happens to after_script?
options: It runs only if allow_failure is true
quiz.explain: after_script always runs after script, success or failure, in a separate shell.

concepts.name: Images, services and default settings
concepts.summary: Pick a Docker image per job, start helper containers like databases with services, and share settings with default.
concepts.why: Tests usually need a specific toolchain and a real database, and services provide both without extra infrastructure.
concepts.body:
With the Docker executor every job runs inside the image named by `image`. Pin a tag (`postgres:17`, `node:22-alpine`) rather than `latest` so pipelines are reproducible. Images can come from Docker Hub, GitLab's own container registry (`$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE`) or any registry the runner can reach.

**Services** are extra containers started alongside the job, typically databases, caches or brokers. The job reaches a service by a hostname derived from the image name (`postgres:17` becomes `postgres`) or by an explicit `alias`. Service containers receive the job's `variables`, which is how you set the database password.

`default:` applies keywords to every job unless a job overrides them: `image`, `services`, `before_script`, `after_script`, `tags`, `retry`, `timeout`, `interruptible` and a few others.

Building Docker images inside a job requires access to a Docker daemon. The common patterns are a `docker:dind` service (Docker-in-Docker, needs a privileged runner) or a daemonless builder such as BuildKit or Kaniko. GitLab provides `$CI_REGISTRY`, `$CI_REGISTRY_USER` and `$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD` so jobs can push to the project's registry without storing credentials.
concepts.code:
default:
  image: python:3.13-slim
  retry: 1

integration:
  services:
    - name: postgres:17
      alias: db
  variables:
    POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test       # also passed to the service container
    DATABASE_URL: postgresql://postgres:test@db:5432/postgres
  script:
    - pip install -r requirements.txt
    - pytest tests/integration

build-image:
  image: docker:28
  services: [docker:28-dind]
  script:
    - docker login -u "$CI_REGISTRY_USER" -p "$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD" "$CI_REGISTRY"
    - docker build -t "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA" .
    - docker push "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA"
takeaways: image sets the job container; pin its tag
services start side containers reachable by name or alias
default: shares image, before_script, retry and more across jobs
pitfalls: Connecting to localhost for a service: with the Docker executor the service has its own hostname.

quiz.q: A job has services: [redis:7]. Which hostname reaches Redis by default?
quiz.explain: The default service alias is derived from the image name without the tag.

concepts.name: CI/CD variables and predefined variables
concepts.summary: Define variables in YAML, use GitLab's predefined CI_ variables, and know the precedence when the same name is set twice.
concepts.why: Variables carry the branch, commit and settings into scripts, and almost every rule and script uses them.
concepts.body:
**Variables** are environment variables available to job scripts. Define them with `variables:` at the top level (all jobs) or inside a job (that job only, overriding the global one).

GitLab sets many **predefined variables** in every job:

- `CI_COMMIT_SHA`, `CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA`: the commit.
- `CI_COMMIT_BRANCH`: the branch name (not set for tag or merge request pipelines); `CI_COMMIT_TAG` for tag pipelines; `CI_COMMIT_REF_NAME` for either.
- `CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH`: usually `main`.
- `CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE`: why the pipeline exists: `push`, `merge_request_event`, `schedule`, `web`, `trigger`, `api`...
- `CI_PROJECT_DIR`, `CI_JOB_ID`, `CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE`, `CI_JOB_TOKEN`.

Variables can also be defined in project, group or instance **settings**, for a schedule, or when running a pipeline manually. When the same name is defined in several places, settings-level and manually supplied variables beat YAML ones, and job-level YAML beats top-level YAML.

Variables can reference other variables (`IMAGE: $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA`). They are expanded by GitLab before the job runs in some keywords (like `image` or `rules`) and by the shell inside `script`. To see what a job receives, run `export` in a debug job, but never in projects with secrets.
concepts.code:
variables:                       # all jobs
  APP_NAME: shop
  IMAGE: $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA

show:
  variables:
    APP_NAME: shop-api            # overrides the global value for this job
  script:
    - echo "$APP_NAME $IMAGE"     # shop-api registry.gitlab.com/acme/shop:1a2b3c4d
    - echo "source=$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE branch=$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH"
    # source=push branch=main
takeaways: variables: at top level or per job; job level wins
CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE and CI_COMMIT_BRANCH drive most logic
Settings and manual variables override YAML variables
pitfalls: Using CI_COMMIT_BRANCH in a merge request pipeline: it is empty there; use CI_COMMIT_REF_NAME or CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_BRANCH_NAME.

quiz.q: Which variable tells you a pipeline was started by a merge request?
quiz.explain: CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE records the trigger; MR pipelines have the value merge_request_event.

concepts.name: Controlling when jobs run with rules
concepts.summary: Use rules with if, changes and exists to add jobs conditionally, make them manual, and control whole pipelines with workflow:rules.
concepts.why: Without rules every job runs on every push; with them you deploy only from main and skip work nobody needs.
concepts.body:
`rules` decides whether a job is added to a pipeline. GitLab evaluates the list **in order** and the first matching rule wins; if none match, the job is **not added**. Each rule can test:

- `if`: an expression over variables, such as `$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH` or `$CI_COMMIT_TAG =~ /^v\d+/`.
- `changes`: file paths or globs changed by the push (`src/**/*`).
- `exists`: files present in the repository.

A matching rule can set `when`: `on_success` (default), `manual` (wait for a click), `delayed` (with `start_in`), `always` or `never`. It can also set `allow_failure` and `variables`.

`when: never` rules are used to exclude cases first, followed by a catch-all. `workflow:rules` uses the same syntax for the **whole pipeline**: if it doesn't match, no pipeline is created. Its most common job is avoiding duplicate pipelines when a branch has an open merge request.

`rules` replaces the older `only` and `except` keywords, which still work but can't be combined with `rules` in the same job. New configuration should use `rules` everywhere.
concepts.code:
workflow:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH && $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS
      when: never                       # avoid branch + MR duplicate pipelines
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH || $CI_COMMIT_TAG

docs:
  script: make docs
  rules:
    - changes: ["docs/**/*"]            # only when docs changed

deploy:
  script: ./deploy.sh
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
      when: manual                      # needs a click on main
    - when: never                       # nowhere else
takeaways: The first matching rule wins; no match means the job is not added
when: manual, delayed, never, always tune the outcome
workflow:rules decides whether a pipeline is created at all
pitfalls: Mixing rules with only/except in the same job, which is a configuration error.

quiz.q: A job has rules: - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG. You push to a branch. What happens to the job?
options: It is not added to the pipeline
It runs because rules default to always
quiz.explain: No rule matched, so the job is excluded from the pipeline.

concepts.name: Artifacts and cache
concepts.summary: Pass build output to later jobs with artifacts, publish test reports, and speed up installs with cache keyed on lockfiles.
concepts.why: Jobs share nothing by default, so artifacts and caches are how pipelines move files and save minutes.
concepts.body:
**Artifacts** are files a job produces that GitLab stores: `artifacts: paths:` lists them and `expire_in` sets how long they're kept. By default, jobs in later stages download the artifacts of all jobs in earlier stages; `dependencies:` or `needs:` restrict that. Artifacts can be browsed and downloaded in the UI.

`artifacts:reports` are special artifacts GitLab understands: `junit` test results show in merge requests, and there are report types for coverage, code quality and security scanners. Use `when: always` so reports upload even when tests fail.

A **cache** stores dependencies between pipelines to avoid re-downloading them. It lives on the runner (or in shared object storage), is best-effort, and is never guaranteed to exist. Configure `cache: key:` and `paths:`; `key: files: [package-lock.json]` changes the key whenever the lockfile changes. `policy: pull` on jobs that only read the cache avoids slow uploads.

The rule: **artifacts** are for passing results between jobs and to people; **cache** is for speeding things up. Never rely on a cache for correctness. Package managers should point their download directory inside the project (for example `PIP_CACHE_DIR: $CI_PROJECT_DIR/.cache/pip`), because only paths inside `$CI_PROJECT_DIR` can be cached or archived.
concepts.code:
variables:
  PIP_CACHE_DIR: $CI_PROJECT_DIR/.cache/pip

test:
  image: python:3.13
  cache:
    key:
      files: [requirements.txt]      # new cache when deps change
    paths: [.cache/pip]
  script:
    - pip install -r requirements.txt
    - pytest --junitxml=report.xml
  artifacts:
    when: always                     # upload even if tests fail
    reports:
      junit: report.xml              # shown in the merge request

build:
  stage: build
  script: [make dist]
  artifacts:
    paths: [dist/]
    expire_in: 1 week
takeaways: Artifacts = outputs for later jobs and humans; cache = speed-up only
Key caches on lockfiles with cache:key:files
Only paths inside $CI_PROJECT_DIR can be cached or archived
pitfalls: Using cache to pass build output to a deploy job; the cache may be missing on another runner.

quiz.q: A deploy job must receive the dist/ folder built two stages earlier. What should the build job use?
quiz.explain: Artifacts are reliably passed to later jobs; caches are best-effort.

concepts.name: needs: faster pipelines as a DAG
concepts.summary: Let jobs start as soon as the jobs they depend on finish, ignoring stage order, and control which artifacts they fetch.
concepts.why: Stage-by-stage pipelines wait for the slowest job; needs can cut total pipeline time dramatically.
concepts.body:
With stages alone, a job waits for **every** job in all earlier stages. `needs:` changes that: a job with `needs: [build-api]` starts as soon as `build-api` succeeds, even if other jobs of earlier stages are still running. The pipeline becomes a **directed acyclic graph** (DAG), visible in the pipeline view as dependency lines.

Details that matter:

- A job with `needs: []` starts immediately when the pipeline is created.
- With `needs`, a job downloads artifacts **only** from the jobs it needs. Use `needs: [{job: build, artifacts: false}]` to wait without downloading.
- If a needed job is not in the pipeline (because its rules excluded it), the pipeline fails to be created, unless the need is marked `optional: true`.
- A job can need up to 50 jobs by default, and can even need jobs in the same stage.

A common use is a monorepo pipeline where frontend and backend each build, test and deploy independently: each chain progresses at its own speed instead of all frontend tests waiting for the slowest backend build.

Stages still matter as a visual grouping and for jobs without `needs`, so most pipelines combine the two.
concepts.code:
stages: [build, test, deploy]

build-api:  {stage: build, script: [make api],  artifacts: {paths: [api/bin/]}}
build-web:  {stage: build, script: [make web],  artifacts: {paths: [web/dist/]}}

test-api:
  stage: test
  needs: [build-api]          # starts when build-api is done, not build-web
  script: [make test-api]

lint:
  stage: test
  needs: []                   # starts immediately
  script: [make lint]

deploy-web:
  stage: deploy
  needs:
    - job: build-web          # gets only web/dist/
    - job: test-api
      artifacts: false
  script: [./deploy-web.sh]
takeaways: needs: lets a job start as soon as its dependencies finish
needs: [] starts a job immediately
With needs, artifacts come only from the needed jobs
pitfalls: Needing a job that rules removed from this pipeline; mark it optional: true.

quiz.q: Job X has needs: [A]. A is in the build stage and finished; B in the build stage is still running. Does X start?
options: Yes, it only waits for A
No, it waits for the whole build stage
Only if X is in the build stage
quiz.explain: needs replaces stage ordering for that job; it waits only for the listed jobs.

concepts.name: Secrets: masked, protected and file variables
concepts.summary: Store credentials as project or group CI/CD variables, mask them in logs, and restrict them to protected branches.
concepts.why: Deploy keys and API tokens must never live in the repository, and must not be readable from every branch.
concepts.body:
Credentials go in **Settings, CI/CD, Variables** at project, group or instance level, never in `.gitlab-ci.yml`. Each variable has options:

- **Masked**: the value is replaced with `[MASKED]` in job logs. Values must meet length and character requirements to be maskable. **Masked and hidden** variables also can't be revealed in the UI after saving.
- **Protected**: only exposed to pipelines on **protected branches or tags**. A developer pushing a feature branch can't read production credentials, because a job on that branch simply doesn't receive them.
- **Environment scope**: only exposed to jobs deploying to a matching environment, such as `production`.
- **Type: File**: GitLab writes the value to a temporary file and the variable contains the **path**. Ideal for kubeconfigs, certificates and service-account JSON.

The **job token** `CI_JOB_TOKEN` is generated per job and lets the job access the package registry, container registry and some APIs of permitted projects; it expires when the job ends. Control which other projects accept it with the token access allowlist.

Masking is a safety net, not a guarantee: base64-encoding or printing part of a secret bypasses it. And anyone who can push to a protected branch can exfiltrate protected variables, so protect branches carefully.
concepts.code:
deploy:
  image: $CI_REGISTRY/acme/tools/kubectl:1.33   # your own tools image
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH   # protected branch
  environment: production
  script:
    # KUBECONFIG is a protected, File-type variable: its value is a path
    - kubectl --kubeconfig "$KUBECONFIG" get nodes
    - ./notify.sh --token "$SLACK_TOKEN"   # masked: logs show [MASKED]

publish-package:
  script:
    - 'curl --header "JOB-TOKEN: $CI_JOB_TOKEN" --upload-file pkg.tgz
       "$CI_API_V4_URL/projects/$CI_PROJECT_ID/packages/generic/pkg/1.0.0/pkg.tgz"'
takeaways: Secrets live in CI/CD settings, not YAML
Protected variables reach only protected branches and tags
File-type variables hold a path to a temporary file
pitfalls: Leaving a deploy secret unprotected so any branch's pipeline can read it.

quiz.q: A protected variable is defined. A developer pushes to feature/x (unprotected). What does their job see?
quiz.explain: Protected variables are only passed to pipelines on protected branches or tags.

concepts.name: include, extends, !reference and components
concepts.summary: Split configuration into files, share templates across projects, inherit job settings with extends, and use CI/CD components.
concepts.why: Large projects and organisations need one maintained pipeline definition instead of copy-paste.
concepts.body:
**include** merges other YAML files into your configuration:

- `include: local: ci/test.yml` from the same repository.
- `include: project: my-group/ci-templates`, `ref: v2`, `file: node.yml` from another project.
- `include: remote:` from a URL, and `include: template:` for GitLab's bundled templates.
- `include: component:` for **CI/CD components**.

**Components** are versioned, reusable pipeline pieces published to the **CI/CD Catalog**. A component declares typed inputs in a `spec:` header and is used as `component: $CI_SERVER_FQDN/my-group/components/python-test@1.2.0` with `inputs:`. Inputs are substituted with `$[[ inputs.name ]]` when the file is included, so they are checked before the pipeline runs.

**Hidden jobs** start with a dot (`.test-base`) and never run; they serve as templates. **extends** inherits from one or more of them, deep-merging hashes. Lists like `script` are **replaced**, not concatenated.

When you need just one piece of another job, **!reference** pulls a specific value: `script: [!reference [.setup, script], make test]` combines lists that extends would overwrite.

Pin includes to tags or SHAs like any dependency, and use the pipeline editor's **Full configuration** view to see the merged result.
concepts.code:
include:
  - local: ci/lint.yml
  - project: acme/ci-templates
    ref: v2.3.0
    file: /templates/python.yml
  - component: $CI_SERVER_FQDN/acme/components/sast@1.4.0
    inputs:
      stage: test

.python-base:                     # hidden job: never runs on its own
  image: python:3.13
  before_script: [pip install -r requirements.txt]
  script: [echo base]

unit:
  extends: .python-base
  script: [pytest tests/unit]     # replaces the base script list

integration:
  extends: .python-base
  script:
    - !reference [.python-base, before_script]
    - pytest tests/integration
takeaways: include pulls in local, project, remote, template and component files
Hidden .jobs plus extends give job templates; lists are replaced
Components are versioned with typed inputs from the CI/CD Catalog
pitfalls: Expecting extends to append to script; it overwrites the list. Use !reference to combine.

quiz.q: A job extends .base, which has script: [a]. The job defines script: [b]. What runs?
quiz.explain: extends deep-merges hashes, but arrays such as script are replaced entirely.

concepts.name: Environments, manual deploys and review apps
concepts.summary: Track deployments with environment:, gate production with manual jobs and protected environments, and spin up review apps per merge request.
concepts.why: Knowing what is deployed where, and who may deploy to production, is central to safe continuous delivery.
concepts.body:
Adding `environment:` to a job records a **deployment** each time it runs. GitLab shows environments under **Operate, Environments** with the currently deployed commit, history and a one-click **re-deploy** of an older successful job for rollbacks.

Key options:

- `name` and `url`: the URL appears as a link in merge requests.
- `deployment_tier`: production, staging, testing, development or other.
- `when: manual` in rules, so production deploys wait for a click.
- **Protected environments** (Settings, CI/CD) restrict who can run deploy jobs and can require approvals.
- `resource_group: production` ensures only one deploy job for that group runs at a time, so two pipelines never deploy concurrently.

**Review apps** are dynamic environments created per branch or merge request, named with variables: `name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG`. A second job with `action: stop` tears it down; link it with `on_stop`, and GitLab runs it when the branch is deleted or the MR merges. `auto_stop_in: 1 week` cleans up forgotten ones.

Environment-scoped variables let the same job script deploy to staging or production with different credentials, chosen by the environment name.
concepts.code:
deploy-review:
  stage: deploy
  script: ./deploy.sh "$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG"
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG
    url: https://$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG.review.example.com
    on_stop: stop-review
    auto_stop_in: 1 week
  rules: [{if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"}]

stop-review:
  stage: deploy
  script: ./teardown.sh "$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG"
  environment: {name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG, action: stop}
  rules: [{if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event", when: manual}]

deploy-prod:
  stage: deploy
  script: ./deploy.sh production
  environment: {name: production, url: https://example.com}
  resource_group: production        # one deploy at a time
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
      when: manual
takeaways: environment: records deployments and enables rollback by re-running old jobs
Protected environments and manual rules gate production
resource_group serializes deploys; on_stop cleans up review apps
pitfalls: Deploying production from two pipelines at once; add a resource_group.

options: Only maintainers can run the job
At most one job in that group runs at a time
The job runs on a production runner
quiz.explain: Jobs sharing a resource group are executed one at a time across pipelines.

concepts.name: Parent-child and multi-project pipelines
concepts.summary: Split big pipelines into child pipelines, generate configuration dynamically, and trigger pipelines in other projects.
concepts.why: Monorepos and multi-service systems outgrow one flat pipeline; downstream pipelines keep them manageable.
concepts.body:
A **trigger job** starts another pipeline instead of running a script.

- **Parent-child pipelines** run in the same project: `trigger: include: path/to/child.yml`. Each child has its own stages and jobs, so a monorepo can have one child per service, each started only when its files change (`rules: changes`).
- **Multi-project pipelines** start a pipeline in another project: `trigger: project: acme/deployer` with an optional `branch`. Useful when an app's pipeline must trigger an infrastructure or end-to-end test project.

By default the trigger job succeeds as soon as the downstream pipeline is **created**. With `strategy: depend` the trigger job waits and mirrors the downstream status, so a failing child fails the parent.

**Dynamic child pipelines** take this further: a job generates a YAML file (from a script, Jsonnet or a template) and saves it as an artifact; the trigger job includes it with `include: - artifact: generated.yml, job: generate`. This lets a pipeline create exactly the jobs needed, such as one per changed package.

Variables pass downstream via `variables:` in the trigger job (`trigger:forward` controls what is forwarded). Child pipelines appear nested in the parent's pipeline graph.
concepts.code:
generate:
  stage: build
  script:
    - ./ci/make-jobs.sh > child.yml    # writes one job per changed package
  artifacts: {paths: [child.yml]}
run-generated:
  stage: test
  trigger:
    include:
      - artifact: child.yml
        job: generate
    strategy: depend                   # parent fails if child fails
backend:
  trigger:
    include: services/backend/.gitlab-ci.yml
    strategy: depend
  rules:
    - changes: ["services/backend/**/*"]
e2e:
  stage: deploy
  variables: {APP_VERSION: $CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA}
  trigger:
    project: acme/e2e-tests
    branch: main
takeaways: trigger:include starts a child pipeline; trigger:project another project's
strategy: depend makes the trigger job mirror the downstream result
Dynamic child pipelines include YAML generated by an earlier job
pitfalls: Forgetting strategy: depend and getting a green parent while the child fails.

quiz.q: Without strategy: depend, when does a trigger job succeed?
options: As soon as the downstream pipeline is created
When all its own scripts pass
quiz.explain: By default the trigger job only waits for the downstream pipeline to be created.

concepts.name: Runners and executors
concepts.summary: Install and register GitLab Runner, choose an executor, route jobs with tags and tune concurrency and autoscaling.
concepts.why: Self-managed runners control cost, hardware, network access and security for every job you run.
concepts.body:
**GitLab Runner** is a Go binary that polls GitLab for jobs and runs them with an **executor**:

- `docker`: each job in a fresh container from the job's `image`; the default choice.
- `kubernetes`: each job as a pod in a cluster; scales with the cluster.
- `shell`: directly on the host; simple but jobs share the machine and its state.
- `docker-autoscaler` and `instance`: create cloud VMs on demand through fleeting plugins; the successor to the deprecated docker+machine autoscaling.

You create a runner in the UI (project, group or instance level), which gives an **authentication token** starting with `glrt-`, then run `gitlab-runner register` with it on the host. The runner's settings live in `config.toml`: `concurrent` caps jobs across the whole process, and each `[[runners]]` section has its executor settings, such as the default image, `privileged` mode and volumes.

Jobs are routed with **tags**: a runner configured with tags `gpu` and `linux` only takes jobs whose `tags:` are a subset of its tags. Runners can also be set to run untagged jobs or only protected branches. A protected runner is the right place for deploy jobs with production access.

Security: `privileged = true` (needed for Docker-in-Docker) gives jobs root-equivalent access to the host. Isolate such runners and never share them with untrusted projects.
concepts.code:
# Register a runner using the glrt- token from the UI
gitlab-runner register --non-interactive \
  --url https://gitlab.example.com \
  --token "$RUNNER_TOKEN" \
  --executor docker --docker-image alpine:3.22

# /etc/gitlab-runner/config.toml (excerpt)
# concurrent = 8                 # max parallel jobs for this process
# [[runners]]
#   name = "docker-gpu"
#   executor = "docker"
#   [runners.docker]
#     image = "alpine:3.22"
#     privileged = false

# .gitlab-ci.yml side: route a job by tags
#   train:
#     tags: [gpu, linux]
gitlab-runner verify && gitlab-runner list
takeaways: The runner polls GitLab; executors decide how jobs are isolated
Tags route jobs; concurrent caps parallel jobs
Privileged runners are root-equivalent; keep them isolated and protected
pitfalls: Using the shell executor for untrusted code; jobs share the host and its leftovers.

quiz.q: A job has tags: [gpu]. Which runner can take it?
options: A runner whose tags include gpu
quiz.explain: A job's tags must be a subset of the runner's tags.

concepts.name: ID tokens, OIDC and pipeline security
concepts.summary: Authenticate to clouds and Vault with id_tokens instead of stored keys, and close the common holes in pipeline security.
concepts.why: Whoever controls your pipeline controls your deploy credentials; keyless auth and protection rules limit the blast radius.
concepts.body:
`id_tokens:` makes GitLab issue a signed **JWT** to the job, with an audience you choose. The token's claims describe the job: `project_path`, `ref`, `ref_protected`, `environment`, `pipeline_source` and a `sub` such as `project_path:acme/shop:ref_type:branch:ref:main`. A cloud provider (AWS, GCP, Azure) or HashiCorp Vault configured to trust your GitLab instance as an OIDC issuer exchanges the token for short-lived credentials. No long-lived keys are stored.

The trust policy is where security lives: require the exact `project_path`, and for production also `ref_protected: true` or a specific environment. Matching only the issuer would let every project on GitLab.com assume your role.

Broader pipeline hardening:

- **Protect** the default and release branches and tags; protected variables, runners and environments all build on that.
- Merge requests from **forks** run pipelines in the fork by default, without your secrets. Running them in the parent project is an explicit, reviewed action.
- `CI_JOB_TOKEN` access is limited by the project's allowlist; keep it tight.
- Pin included templates and components to versions; an attacker who can change a shared template changes every pipeline that includes it.
- Treat `.gitlab-ci.yml` changes as security-sensitive and use code owners for them.
concepts.code:
deploy:
  image:
    name: amazon/aws-cli:2.27.0
    entrypoint: [""]           # the image's entrypoint is aws
  id_tokens:
    AWS_TOKEN:
      aud: sts.amazonaws.com
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
  environment: production
  script:
    - >
      export $(printf "AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=%s AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=%s AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=%s"
      $(aws sts assume-role-with-web-identity
      --role-arn "$ROLE_ARN" --role-session-name "gl-$CI_JOB_ID"
      --web-identity-token "$AWS_TOKEN" --duration-seconds 3600
      --query 'Credentials.[AccessKeyId,SecretAccessKey,SessionToken]' --output text))
    - aws sts get-caller-identity
# AWS trust policy condition (excerpt):
# "gitlab.example.com:sub": "project_path:acme/shop:ref_type:branch:ref:main"
takeaways: id_tokens issue a per-job JWT for keyless cloud or Vault login
Restrict trust to project_path and protected refs
Protected branches underpin protected variables, runners and environments
pitfalls: A trust policy that only checks the issuer and audience, trusting every project on the instance.

quiz.q: Which claim condition best ensures only main-branch jobs of acme/shop get production credentials?
quiz.explain: sub encodes both the project and the ref; aud and iss alone match every project.

concepts.name: Merge request pipelines and merge trains
concepts.summary: Understand branch vs merge request vs merged results pipelines, and how merge trains keep main green under heavy merge traffic.
concepts.why: Busy repositories break main when individually green MRs conflict; the right pipeline type prevents that.
concepts.body:
GitLab can create several kinds of pipeline for the same commit, and the difference matters:

- **Branch pipelines** run on the pushed commit, with `CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == push`. They can access protected variables only on protected branches.
- **Merge request pipelines** (`merge_request_event`) run on the MR's source branch commit when it is opened or updated. Jobs need rules that match this source. They expose `CI_MERGE_REQUEST_*` variables such as the IID and target branch.
- **Merged results pipelines** run on a temporary commit that merges the source into the **current** target branch, so tests see the code as it would be after merging.
- **Merge trains** queue MRs. Each MR's pipeline runs on the target branch plus every MR ahead of it in the train. If one fails, it is removed and the ones behind it restart. When each pipeline passes, its MR merges in order, so main stays green even with many concurrent merges.

Without `workflow:rules` a push to a branch with an open MR can create both a branch pipeline and an MR pipeline, doubling cost. The `$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH && $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS` never-rule prevents that.

Merged results pipelines and merge trains are Premium features and require the project setting to be enabled; `interruptible: true` lets superseded pipelines be cancelled automatically to save runner time.
concepts.code:
workflow:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH && $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS
      when: never
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH

default:
  interruptible: true            # cancel superseded pipelines

test:
  script:
    - echo "MR !$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID into $CI_MERGE_REQUEST_TARGET_BRANCH_NAME"
    - make test
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH

deploy:
  interruptible: false           # never cancel a deploy midway
  script: [./deploy.sh]
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
takeaways: Branch, MR, merged results and merge train pipelines test different commits
Merge trains test each MR on top of the ones queued ahead of it
workflow:rules prevents duplicate branch + MR pipelines
pitfalls: Writing rules only for branch pipelines, so jobs silently vanish from MR pipelines.

quiz.q: Two MRs each pass their own pipeline but break main when both merge. What prevents this?
options: Merge trains, which test each MR on top of the ones ahead of it
quiz.explain: Merge trains validate the combination of queued changes before they merge.
